task_description: Integrate Taskboard for local development and CI: multi-stage Dockerfiles for the Python API (uv, python slim) and the Node UI (node alpine) running as non-root; a docker-compose.yml running ui, api, a one-shot migrate job, PostgreSQL 16 and Redis 7 where only the UI port is published; a least-privilege PostgreSQL application role created by a management command; a .env.example with placeholder secrets; a Makefile; a bash smoke test that drives the UI with curl (register, login, CSRF tokens, upload/download); and a GitHub Actions CI workflow running lint, type checks, tests with PostgreSQL and Redis service containers, and Terraform checks.

threats.name: API keys or passwords are committed to the repo or baked into code
Attacker input changes the meaning of a database query
Passwords are stored in plain text or with a fast hash, so a database leak exposes them
Debug features or consoles are left on in production
Default or hardcoded admin accounts are left active
.env, .git, or backup files are reachable from the web
A database, cache, or admin port is reachable from the internet
An AI-suggested package does not exist, and an attacker can register that name
Encryption or signing keys are hardcoded or shared across environments
A request sets fields the user should not control, such as role or price
Query operators in user input bypass filters in a NoSQL database
Cloud roles or service accounts allow far more than the app needs
Secrets are copied into the image or passed as build arguments
Sensitive fields are stored unencrypted, so a backup or database leak exposes them
Queries miss the tenant filter, so customers see each other's data
A lookalike package name installs malicious code
A library with a known CVE is used in a reachable code path
The coding agent can read .env files, SSH keys, or cloud credentials
The container runs as root, so an app flaw becomes host-level access
The app connects as an admin database user, so any flaw becomes full data access

countermeasures.name: Load secrets from a secrets manager or environment
countermeasures.how_to: Keep secrets out of code, images, and the repo. Use environment variables or a vault, scope access narrowly, and rotate anything that leaked.

countermeasures.name: Use parameterized queries or an ORM
countermeasures.how_to: Pass user values as parameters. Never build SQL or query documents by joining strings.

countermeasures.name: Hash passwords with a slow, salted algorithm
countermeasures.how_to: Use Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt through your framework's password helper. Never use MD5 or SHA for passwords.

countermeasures.name: Turn debug features off in production
countermeasures.how_to: Set DEBUG false, remove debug consoles and verbose logging, and fail the deploy if debug is on.

countermeasures.name: Remove default and hardcoded accounts
countermeasures.how_to: Ship no preset admin users. Create the first admin through a one-time setup step with a strong generated password.

countermeasures.name: Do not deploy repo metadata or env files
countermeasures.how_to: Exclude .git, .env, and backups from the build and the web root, and block them at the web server.

countermeasures.name: Keep data stores off the public internet
countermeasures.how_to: Place databases and caches in private subnets, bind them to internal interfaces, and allow only the app through security groups.

countermeasures.name: Check every new package exists and is the one you meant
countermeasures.how_to: Confirm the name, age, and publisher on the registry before installing, and watch for lookalike names.

countermeasures.name: Use separate keys per environment and rotate them
countermeasures.how_to: Generate different keys for development, staging, and production, load them from the secrets manager, and rotate them on a schedule or after exposure.

countermeasures.name: Accept only the fields you expect
countermeasures.how_to: Bind requests to an explicit schema or DTO with allowed fields. Never copy a request body straight onto a model.

countermeasures.name: Check permissions on the server for every action
countermeasures.how_to: Enforce role and permission checks in a central layer on each endpoint, not only by hiding UI.

countermeasures.name: Validate all input on the server
countermeasures.how_to: Check type, length, range, and format for every input on the server. Client-side checks are only for convenience.

countermeasures.name: Grant only the cloud permissions the app uses
countermeasures.how_to: Write narrow roles per service, avoid wildcards on actions and resources, and review them when features change.

countermeasures.name: Encrypt sensitive data at rest
countermeasures.how_to: Use AES-GCM or your cloud provider's managed encryption, with keys held outside the database.

countermeasures.name: Scope every query to the tenant
countermeasures.how_to: Apply the tenant filter in one place, such as a query helper or row-level security, so no query can forget it.

countermeasures.name: Pin versions and commit lockfiles
countermeasures.how_to: Commit a lockfile, install with the frozen or locked option in CI, and review dependency changes in pull requests.

countermeasures.name: Scan dependencies and update vulnerable ones
countermeasures.how_to: Scan lockfiles for known vulnerabilities, fix reachable ones first, and keep updates on a regular schedule.

countermeasures.name: Keep secrets out of the agent's reach
countermeasures.how_to: Deny reads of .env files, SSH keys, and cloud credentials in the agent's permission rules, and use scoped short-lived credentials.

countermeasures.name: Run containers as non-root on minimal images
countermeasures.how_to: Set a non-root USER, use a slim or distroless base image, and drop extra capabilities.

countermeasures.name: Give the app a least-privilege database account
countermeasures.how_to: Create a user limited to the tables and operations the app needs. Keep migrations on a separate admin account.

assessment.summary: 20 threats and 20 countermeasures for container-and-iac, secrets-and-config, database, dependencies. Risk level critical (highest threat severity, raised for sensitive data).

instructions: Build these countermeasures in as you write the code, starting with the most severe threats. These threats come from the components you picked. also_consider lists general threats from implied components; pass those components explicitly for full detail. After writing code, call general_verify_code_security with the same components.
